blogs.title: You Can’t Shrink the Marketplace Mid-Analysis: The Federal Circuit Demands Consistent Scope Across DuPont Factors
blogs.description: The court’s central move was to fault the TTAB for treating the parties’ services as “highly similar—indeed, partially legally identical” under DuPont factor 2, yet narrowing the relevant field under factor 6 to only credit card services when assessing third‑party use. This post unpacks why that mismatch is legally significant, how it builds on Olde Tyme Foods, Juice Generation, and Jack Wolfskin, and what it means for proving (or rebutting) commercial weakness. We’ll offer practice pointers for making a broader third‑party record when services overlap (e.g., credit cards, banking, financing) and discuss how the decision pressures the Board to harmonize the scope of “similarity” across factors rather than toggling between narrow and broad frames.

blogs.title: What Counts as “Credit Card Services” When the ID Manual Entry Is Gone? Legacy Identifications, Fintech Structures, and Factor 2
blogs.description: Affirming the TTAB on factor 2, the Federal Circuit blessed the Board’s expansive reading of “credit card services” to include issuing cards, processing transactions, account management, authorization, and related alerts—even though the Trademark ID Manual entry had been deleted years after CC Serve’s 1998 registration. This post explores how tribunals can construe legacy identifications, the weight given to dictionary sources and industry practice, and why a non‑bank program manager partnering with a bank can still land in “legally identical, in part” territory vis‑à‑vis a bank applicant. We consider the decision’s implications for fintech program managers, banks white‑labeling products, and applicants drafting service descriptions that either cabin or expand relatedness.

blogs.title: Strength Bleeds Into Similarity: Why Vacating Factor 6 Forced a Do‑Over on Factor 1
blogs.description: By vacating the factor 6 analysis, the panel also vacated factor 1, emphasizing that commercial impression cannot be evaluated in a vacuum divorced from marketplace strength or weakness. This post examines the court’s reasoning that the perceived strength of ASPIRE—once the broader field of banking and financing third‑party uses is considered—may recalibrate how similar ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK feel in the eyes of consumers. We discuss the doctrinal intertwining of strength and similarity, how evidence of a crowded field can narrow the range of protection for a common term, and what advocates should do on remand: build a robust record of third‑party use across all similar financial services, not just credit cards.

blogs.title: TTAB Litigation in a Crowded Financial Marketplace: Building the Right Record After Apex v. CC Serve
blogs.description: This practical post distills takeaways for brand owners and challengers in financial services. Key lessons: align your similarity frame across DuPont factors; marshal third‑party uses and registrations across the full spectrum of similar services (banking, lending, credit cards, payments); don’t assume program‑manager structures insulate you from relatedness; and be ready to show how field crowding shapes consumer education and narrows scope. We also flag strategic implications for intent‑to‑use applications in common financial terms, the value (and limits) of ID Manual entries and dictionaries, and how to position evidence so that factor 6 informs factor 1 rather than getting compartmentalized.
